papers.title: Effective strain energy of soft laminates: Beyond neo-Hookean elasticity
papers.abstract: Composite laminates can be designed to reach desired engineering properties such as low weight and high stiffness. This study concerns periodic media made of alternating layers of soft rubber-like solids. Assuming incompressible and perfectly bonded elastic layers, the effective mechanical response of the laminate is estimated by means of homogenisation theory. This involves computing the spatial average of the energy stored in the layers, each of which is in equilibrium and homogeneously deformed. The study is conducted for layers whose elastic energy depends on two scalar invariants, in general. Beyond neo-Hookean solids, explicit analytical expressions are obtained for a special class of Mooney-Rivlin materials, whereas approximate expressions are obtained for Mooney-Rivlin laminates and for Yeoh laminates. These stratified media can be represented by a transversely isotropic elasticity theory at the macroscopic scale. Based on these results, an approximate effective energy for laminates whose layers combine Gent-type and Mooney-Rivlin behaviour is postulated. It is then used to estimate the macroscopic instability threshold under pure shear numerically. Results show that the specific mechanical response of individual layers has negligible influence on the macroscopic stability limit if a certain proportionality relationship between their energy functions holds. Furthermore, in a pre-stressed layered medium under pure shear, the influence of the individual mechanical response of the layers on the shear wave velocity is found to be comparable to that observed in homogeneous media, within the same range of investigated situations. Finally, more significant effects may be observed in non-proportional laminates.

papers.title: Relative periodic orbits of a free spinning loop
papers.abstract: A closed elastic string with no external forces can hold any shape while its material moves steadily along the curve (a steady axial motion), because its tension and the force needed to turn the material around a bend are both proportional to the curvature. I compute the periodic motions that grow from the simplest of these motions, the spinning ring, by Newton's method on a chain of masses. They include rotating waves that turn at twice the rotation rate of the material, standing "flappers" with two to five lobes, and period-doubled and period-tripled orbits. The chain only approximates the string. The orbits and their strong instabilities change little with more masses and are properties of the continuous string. Most weak instabilities change with the number of masses and are artifacts of approximating the string by a finite chain. The saddle flapper of a loop stretched 30% beyond its natural length is neutrally stable at small heights and unstable at large ones. An unstable saddle flapper trades energy back and forth with an in-plane oval, and at large amplitude the energy spreads to the shortest waves of the chain. For Keller's linear string, whose tension is proportional to the stretched length, every motion is periodic, and every knot carries an exactly periodic flapper. For a Hookean string the curvature of a knot couples a ripple to stretching waves that travel at a different speed, and in the simulations a ripple on a sliding knot does not return to its starting shape. Whether a Hookean knot carries any periodic flapper is open.

papers.title: Euler-Lagrange Equations Formulated in Terms of Angular Velocity
papers.abstract: We propose a novel variant of the Euler--Lagrange (EL) equation for rigid body rotation, explicitly formulated in terms of orientation parameters $\thh$ and angular velocity $\omm$. Variational analysis of the stationarity condition of the action integral for a Lagrangian in terms of $\thh$ and $\omm$ yields a modified EL formulation. For pure rotational motion, the proposed equation directly recovers equations of motion fully consistent with the classical Euler equations, bypassing explicit geometry-based torque analysis. Furthermore, the framework seamlessly accommodates coupled translational and rotational dynamics, as validated through a spring-suspended symmetrical top, exhibiting exact agreement with the Newton--Euler equations. We also identify an inherent discrepancy in the standard EL approach, demonstrating that applying a direct coordinate transformation $\dot\thh\mapsto\omm$ causes the resulting formulation to deviate from both the classical Euler equation and our proposed formulation. The proposed framework is expected to provide an intuitive, versatile modeling tool for spatial rigid body dynamics.

papers.title: Reactive Phase Change of a Single Droplet in Turbulent Flow with Reactive Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium Using a Two-Scalar Diffusive-Interface Method
papers.abstract: Reactive phase change fluids have been shown to enhance thermodynamic performance by integrating chemical reactions with thermodynamic cycles. This study investigates the turbulent evaporation of a single droplet using Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) to model the behavior of reactive phase change fluids. Applying Reactive Vapor--Liquid Equilibrium (RVLE) thermodynamics, the study simultaneously captures the dynamics of reactive phase transitions, mass transfer, and heat transfer during the evaporation of dinitrogen tetroxide (N___O___). A second-order phase field framework is used to derive two scalar transport equations, accurately describing species behavior at equilibrium. The equilibrium is maintained by balancing concentration exchange rates across both the liquid-to-vapor and vapor-to-liquid phases. Results indicate that chemical reactivity significantly influences phase transition dynamics, altering the phase dome structure by modifying critical points and the thermodynamic saturation lines. Endothermic and exothermic behaviors are observed at the interface during the fast reversible evaporation process of N___O___(l) ___ 2NO___(v,l). Turbulence simulations further show enhanced mixing efficiency and improved gas-liquid separation, driven by chaotic flow patterns. This study elucidates the role of reactive phase change fluids in contrast to conventional non-reactive phase flows, emphasizing the influence of chemical reactions on phase transition dynamics and overall system performance..

papers.title: Bandgap fluctuations and robustness in two-dimensional hyperuniform dielectric materials
papers.abstract: We numerically study the statistical fluctuations of photonic band gaps in ensembles of stealthy hyperuniform disordered patterns. We find that at low stealthiness, where correlations are weak, band gaps of different system realizations appear over a wide frequency range, are narrow, and generally do not overlap. Interestingly, above a critical value of stealthiness $\chi \gtrsim 0.35$, the bandgaps become large and overlap significantly from realization to realization, while a second gap appears. These observations extend our understanding of photonic bandgaps in disordered systems and provide information on the robustness of gaps in practical applications.

papers.title: Memory-like effects and kinematics of trajectories in Cyclotron motion
papers.abstract: We investigate the collective dynamics of a bundle of charged particles undergoing cyclotron motion in a uniform magnetic field when subjected to a short-duration electric pulse. Using the geometric framework based on the evolution of trajectory congruences, we analyze how the pulse affects the expansion, shear, and rotation of a small family of trajectories. We show that the geometric imprint persists after the pulse has vanished, manifesting as a memory of the transient perturbation. Unlike gravitational memory effects, this does not manifest itself in focusing behaviour of the trajectories, and instead implies a restructuring of the shear component before and after the pulse. We offer direct analytic and regression based arguments for the same.
